steps.intent: Greece’s objectives are to restore deterrence against Houthi attacks, protect freedom of navigation and seafarers, reinforce the 2216 arms embargo, and keep the Council focused on a UN-led Yemen peace process. The main difficulty will be balancing strong condemnation of Houthi attacks with enough restraint and root-cause language to avoid Russian or Chinese vetoes and secure at least nine votes. We expect negotiations over references to the broader regional conflict, the defensive actions of Member States, and the reporting mandate.

messages.Algeria: Algeria supports the draft’s condemnation of attacks on shipping, demands for release of detained personnel, and its humanitarian and political tracks. However, we cannot accept a text that reaffirms a self-defence right without clearly excluding any authorization for the use of force against the territory of Yemen or other States, and we need an explicit Gaza ceasefire and root-cause reference. We also ask that the political process be described as Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned.
messages.China: China supports a clear Council message that Houthi attacks must stop and that humanitarian access and detained personnel must be addressed. However, the current text’s repeated reaffirmation of the right to defend vessels, without precise qualifiers, risks being misinterpreted as endorsing military action and further escalation. China therefore requests that PP5 and OP5 be revised to require full compliance with international law and the Charter, respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and coastal States, and avoidance of escalation; OP4 should also expressly exclude unilateral enforcement measures. China can support the text with these changes.
messages.Denmark: Denmark supports the draft and thanks Greece and the United States for a balanced text. We ask for two strengthening edits: OP6 should reference international human rights law alongside international humanitarian law, and OP7 should make the political settlement explicitly inclusive and ensure women's full, equal and meaningful participation. These reflect Denmark's consistent conflict-prevention and human-rights priorities, and we are ready to join consensus with these adjustments.
messages.France: France supports the draft’s clear condemnation of Houthi attacks and its demand that attacks cease and detained personnel be released. We ask the penholder to strengthen OP3 and OP6 on arbitrary detention, the inviolability of UN premises, international human rights law and full humanitarian access, and to make OP7’s root-causes language include the conflict in Gaza. These points are important for France’s support and would improve the text’s balance without weakening its message against the Houthis.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the thrust of the draft and welcomes the co-penholders' efforts. We continue to believe the Council must address root causes, including the conflict in Gaza, and would ask that the text explicitly recall the call for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and compliance with international law and relevant Council resolutions. With that change, we can support the text.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the draft’s clear condemnation of attacks on merchant and commercial vessels and its call for humanitarian access and a UN-led political process. We ask for balanced language reaffirming non-intervention and ensuring that maritime security efforts respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the coastal States and do not escalate tensions. We also believe the root-causes paragraph should explicitly include the situation in Gaza, given its link to regional escalation.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the draft's condemnation and demands, reflecting our strong interest in maritime security and the safety of seafarers. We ask the penholder to anchor OP4 and OP5 explicitly in UNCLOS and flag State jurisdiction and to include the IMO and seafarer welfare in cooperation and reporting. Panama would not support any language that creates an open-ended authorization for the use of force or undermines flag State responsibilities.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the draft as circulated. We welcome its strong condemnation of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels, its clear demand for the release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and detained United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers, and its reaffirmation of the arms embargo and freedom of navigation. As a maritime trading nation, the Republic of Korea attaches great importance to safe navigation and global supply chains, and we believe this text sends a timely and balanced message. We encourage all Council members to support its adoption.
messages.Russian Federation: The Russian Federation supports the goal of safe navigation but cannot accept the current text as it repeats flawed provisions of resolution 2722 (2024) that could be used to justify illegal US/UK/Israeli strikes against Yemen. We request deletion of the UNCLOS reference and the self-defense language in PP5 and OP5, replacing them with strict adherence to the UN Charter and an explicit statement that nothing authorizes military action against Yemen or any other State. We also insist on including the Gaza ceasefire and a balanced condemnation of attacks on Yemen's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks Greece and the co-sponsors for their constructive work and supports the draft's strong condemnation of Houthi attacks on maritime and civilian targets. To be consistent with our previous calls on this file, we ask that the text explicitly recognise the situation in Gaza in the context of root causes and broader regional tensions, and that the Secretary-General's reporting cover such regional developments. These additions would strengthen the Council's credibility and its ability to address the root causes of the crisis.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the draft's clear condemnation of Houthi attacks and its focus on maritime security, the arms embargo and the Yemen peace process. We ask that OP5 be tightened to make clear that any defence of vessels is exercised within international law, including international humanitarian and human rights law and the strict conditions of self-defence, and that OP6 and OP8 reflect human rights and humanitarian access reporting. With those changes, Slovenia can support the text.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the draft's clear condemnation of Houthi attacks and its emphasis on the UN-led political process. We ask that OP5 explicitly reaffirm respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Red Sea coastal States, and that a new operative paragraph call for international support to regional maritime capacity-building, including counter-piracy. These changes would strengthen regional ownership without altering the text's core.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom strongly supports the draft as presented. It clearly condemns the Houthi attacks, demands that they cease, calls for the release of the Galaxy Leader and detained UN and humanitarian personnel, and reinforces the arms embargo and freedom of navigation. We welcome the continued reporting request and urge the Council to adopt this text swiftly.
messages.United States of America: The United States fully supports the draft as circulated and is proud to co-sponsor it. It strongly condemns Houthi attacks, reaffirms the right of Member States to defend their vessels, and reinforces the arms embargo and UN-led peace process. We urge all Council members to join consensus and send a unified message to the Houthis.

replies.Algeria: partially accepted: Gaza ceasefire and regional-linkage language added, OP5 safeguards and OP7 Gaza references included, but OP5 preserves law-based vessel protection and OP7 uses an inclusive Yemeni-led formulation.
replies.China: partially accepted: OP5 qualified and OP6 restraint added, OP4 and OP8 partly reflect requests, but the explicit no-pretext clause was not included in full.
replies.Denmark: accepted: OP7 includes an inclusive settlement and women's full, equal and meaningful participation; OP6 includes human rights law.
replies.France: accepted: OP3, OP6, OP7 and OP8 strengthened on arbitrary detention, UN premises, human rights, Gaza and reporting as requested.
replies.Guyana: accepted: a preambular paragraph on an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and its link to regional tensions was added.
replies.Pakistan: accepted: non-intervention, coastal-State sovereignty, and Gaza root-cause language were included.
replies.Panama: partially accepted: UNCLOS, flag State jurisdiction, IMO cooperation and seafarer reporting were included, but Article 51 was not expressly cited.
replies.Republic of Korea: accepted: no changes requested; the draft retains strong condemnation, maritime security and arms-embargo language.
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: PP2 and PP5 were revised and OP5 limits authorization, and Gaza linkage was added; however, a named condemnation of US, UK and Israeli strikes on Yemen was rejected.
replies.Sierra Leone: accepted: Gaza was included in root causes and regional developments are now covered in reporting.
replies.Slovenia: partially accepted: OP5 now includes strict self-defence and IHL/IHRL language, while OP6 and OP8 add accountability and reporting elements, though not as exact replacements.
replies.Somalia: accepted: coastal-State sovereignty was reaffirmed and a maritime capacity-building paragraph was added.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: accepted: no changes requested; core condemnation of Houthi attacks and maritime-security provisions were retained.
replies.United States of America: accepted: no changes requested; the text preserves the core condemnation of Houthi attacks, arms embargo and maritime security focus.

steps.summary: The revision accommodates key non-permanent members through Gaza-linkage, humanitarian, human-rights, sovereignty and reporting language while preserving the core condemnation of Houthi attacks. It modifies self-defence-related language and avoids naming US/UK/Israeli strikes, aiming to secure Russian and Chinese abstentions rather than vetoes. The text is expected to command broad support with no negative P5 vote.

messages.Algeria: Algeria welcomes the inclusion of the Gaza ceasefire and regional-linkage language, as well as the OP5 safeguards confirming that nothing in this resolution authorizes the use of force against the territory of any State. We can support this text if the ceasefire reference is strengthened to an 'immediate and permanent ceasefire', consistent with our long-standing position. We thank the penholder for the constructive engagement and urge retention of the sovereignty and restraint language.
messages.China: China supports the current text. We appreciate that the penholder has incorporated our core concerns, particularly the clarifications in PP5 and OP5 that measures to protect vessels must conform to international law, fully respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and coastal States, and that nothing in this resolution authorizes the use of force against the territory of any State, together with OP7's call for restraint. While the explicit no-pretext clause in OP4 was not included in full, OP5 addresses our principal concern. China therefore supports the draft and encourages Council unity and a comprehensive political solution, including an immediate ceasefire in Gaza.
messages.Denmark: Denmark welcomes the revised text and the incorporation of international human rights law and the full, equal and meaningful participation of women. The draft provides a balanced, law-based response to Houthi attacks while reaffirming Yemen’s sovereignty, humanitarian access, freedom of navigation and the UN-led peace process. Denmark supports the text as it stands and calls for its adoption.
messages.France: France supports the current text and thanks the penholder for incorporating our proposals on arbitrary detention, UN premises, international human rights law, Gaza and reporting. The text provides a balanced basis for adoption: it condemns Houthi attacks, upholds freedom of navigation, respects sovereignty and international law, and calls for restraint and humanitarian access. We have no further requests and encourage the Council to proceed to a vote.
messages.Guyana: Guyana supports the current draft and appreciates the penholders' constructive engagement, including the addition of language on an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and its link to regional tensions. The text appropriately condemns the Houthi attacks, demands the release of the Galaxy Leader crew and detained UN personnel, reaffirms the arms embargo, and stresses full respect for international law, sovereignty and UNCLOS. Guyana will vote in favour of the draft as it stands.
messages.Pakistan: Pakistan supports the revised draft and welcomes the incorporation of non-intervention, sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and the Red Sea coastal States, as well as the Gaza root-cause language. We encourage full respect for international law and the Charter, and we stress that all measures must avoid further escalation and remain consistent with the protection of civilians and unhindered humanitarian access.
messages.Panama: Panama supports the current text. It reflects our priorities on UNCLOS, flag State jurisdiction, IMO cooperation, protection of seafarers and freedom of navigation, and it preserves a strict international-law framework for any measures at sea. We can accept the absence of an explicit Article 51 citation, as the reference to self-defence under international law is sufficient, and we encourage the Council to speak with unity.
messages.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea supports the revised draft as it stands. It maintains a strong condemnation of Houthi attacks, demands the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and detained UN personnel, and reinforces full implementation of the targeted arms embargo. We also welcome the emphasis on freedom of navigation, seafarer safety, humanitarian access, and a UN-led political process in Yemen. The Republic of Korea is ready to vote in favour of this text.
messages.Russian Federation: We note that the revised text partially takes account of our concerns, including on Gaza and on limiting authorization. However, references to UNCLOS and self-defence language remain unacceptable because they can be misused to justify military action against Yemen. We can support the text only if the red lines above are addressed; we also continue to insist that the Council cannot condemn only one side while ignoring strikes by the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel against Yemeni territory.
messages.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks Greece and the United States for the revised text and welcomes the inclusion of the situation in Gaza in the root causes and reporting provisions, as we requested. The text reflects our priorities: condemning Houthi attacks, protecting freedom of navigation and seafarers, respecting sovereignty and international law, supporting Yemen's peace process and humanitarian access. We support the draft as it stands and encourage all Council members to unite behind it.
messages.Slovenia: Slovenia thanks Greece and the co-sponsors for the revised text. The current draft incorporates our key concerns on strict self-defence, international humanitarian and human rights law, accountability, and human rights reporting. As a maritime State, Slovenia strongly supports freedom of navigation and condemns the Houthi attacks, while stressing that all measures must respect sovereignty and international law. We support the text as it stands and encourage the Council to speak with one voice.
messages.Somalia: Somalia supports the revised draft and appreciates the incorporation of coastal-State sovereignty and maritime capacity-building for the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. We urge the Council to speak with one voice in condemning attacks on shipping, protecting humanitarian access, and advancing the UN-led political process in Yemen.
messages.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The United Kingdom supports the Council’s clear condemnation of Houthi attacks and the maritime-security provisions in this draft. We ask the penholder to adjust the Gaza linkage so that it cannot be read as justifying the Houthis’ illegal attacks, and to reaffirm Article 51 self-defence in OP5. We also propose that OP7 focus on all parties and international law rather than a general call on Member States that could be misread as constraining lawful self-defence.
messages.United States of America: We appreciate Greece's work and can support the text with targeted adjustments. We need an explicit affirmation of the right of Member States to defend their vessels and personnel, and we cannot accept language that could be read as constraining lawful responses to Houthi attacks. We also ask that the Gaza reference not be framed as a clear link that could be invoked to justify Houthi attacks; the text should make clear such attacks are unjustified.

replies.China: accepted: no-force, sovereignty and restraint language retained; no specific change requested.
replies.Denmark: accepted: human rights, women’s participation and law-based approach retained.
replies.France: accepted: detention, UN premises, Gaza and reporting provisions retained.
replies.Guyana: accepted: ceasefire, Houthi condemnation, arms embargo and international law retained.
replies.Pakistan: accepted: sovereignty, non-intervention and Gaza root-cause language retained.
replies.Panama: partially accepted: IMO, seafarer and freedom-of-navigation language retained, but explicit UNCLOS/flag-State references were removed to preserve consensus.
replies.Republic of Korea: accepted: Houthi condemnation, release demands, embargo and political process retained.
replies.Russian Federation: partially accepted: UNCLOS/protecting-vessels references removed from the preamble and OP4, Gaza ceasefire added, and unlawful strikes against Yemeni territory addressed generically; its red line on self-defence and naming the United States, United Kingdom and Israel was not accepted.
replies.Sierra Leone: accepted: Gaza included in root causes and reporting; maritime security balanced with sovereignty.
replies.Slovenia: accepted: strict self-defence, IHL/IHRL, accountability and human-rights reporting retained.
replies.Somalia: accepted: coastal-State sovereignty, maritime capacity-building and unity language retained.
replies.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: accepted: Article 51 self-defence reaffirmed, OP7 refocused on all parties, and Gaza language clarified that Houthi attacks are unjustified.
replies.United States of America: accepted: explicit right to defend vessels and personnel included, OP7 adjusted, and Gaza linkage clarified that Houthi attacks cannot be justified.

steps.summary: The revision balances Russian concerns through removal of explicit UNCLOS/flag-State language, a generic condemnation of unlawful strikes on Yemeni territory, and a Gaza ceasefire operative paragraph, while retaining core US/UK priorities on self-defence and vessel protection. Greece as penholder presents a consensus text expected to secure broad support, with Russia likely abstaining rather than vetoing.

reasons.Algeria: Algeria had requested permanent ceasefire language on Gaza, which was accepted, and the text now includes its core concerns on sovereignty, non-use of force and root causes. With these improvements, Algeria can support the resolution.
reasons.China: The draft incorporates China’s core concerns—no authorization of force, respect for sovereignty, restraint, and a Gaza ceasefire—while addressing attacks on shipping, so China supports it.
reasons.Denmark: Denmark’s foreign policy strongly favours multilateral crisis management, international law, humanitarian access, and support for UN-led peace processes; the draft reflects these priorities and is sufficiently balanced to merit a yes vote.
reasons.France: France has consistently supported balanced Council action on Red Sea maritime security, Houthi attacks, arms embargo compliance, and Yemen’s political process. The draft accommodates France’s emphasis on international law, sovereignty, restraint, humanitarian access, and Gaza without triggering opposition.
reasons.Greece: Greece co-sponsored the draft and, as a shipping and EU/NATO member, prioritizes freedom of navigation, international law and maritime security; the balanced text strongly condemns Houthi attacks while reaffirming sovereignty and self-defence without authorizing force.
reasons.Guyana: Guyana has consistently supported Council action condemning Houthi attacks while insisting on international law, sovereignty, and a Gaza ceasefire, and the penholder accepted its key concerns. A pre-vote explanation clarifies that Guyana's support for maritime security is not an endorsement of unlawful military strikes.
reasons.Pakistan: Pakistan indicated support in the last negotiation round; the draft retains sovereignty, non-intervention and Gaza root-cause language consistent with Pakistan’s established positions while condemning Houthi attacks on shipping. A yes vote with an explanation is the most consistent course.
reasons.Panama: Panama supports the resolution as consistent with its maritime and international-law priorities, especially freedom of navigation, protection of seafarers, and peaceful settlement. Despite preferring explicit UNCLOS language, it backs the compromise to maintain Council consensus.
reasons.Republic of Korea: The Republic of Korea’s established position condemns Houthi attacks on shipping, supports freedom of navigation, the arms embargo and a UN-led Yemen process, and the balanced draft is consistent with those interests and its prior votes. Seoul would therefore vote in favour.
reasons.Russian Federation: The draft reflects several Russian amendments but retains the self-defence/protecting-vessels language Moscow identified as a red line and does not name the US, UK, or Israel for strikes on Yemen. Russia would likely abstain rather than veto, consistent with its prior abstentions on Red Sea resolutions.
reasons.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone has consistently supported Council action on maritime security while emphasizing root causes, international law and Yemeni sovereignty; the revised draft reflects those priorities and the accepted balance on Gaza and sovereignty. Voting in favour is therefore consistent with its prior record and requests in negotiations.
reasons.Slovenia: Slovenia supports the draft because it clearly condemns Houthi attacks, upholds freedom of navigation, and retains strict references to international law, self-defence, accountability and humanitarian reporting consistent with its positions. It has no need to make a pre-vote explanation.
reasons.Somalia: Somalia’s last negotiation position was support, and the final text aligns with its priorities on maritime security, sovereignty, non-intervention, humanitarian access, and a UN-led Yemen peace process. It will therefore vote in favour and explain its support.
reasons.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: The revised text incorporates the UK’s key requested changes: it clarifies that Houthi attacks are unjustified by Gaza, reaffirms Article 51 self-defence, and refocuses language on all parties. This is consistent with the UK’s record of condemning Houthi attacks and supporting freedom of navigation without undermining lawful self-defence.
reasons.United States of America: The United States co-sponsored the draft and secured its key red line on self-defence and protection of vessels and personnel, so it would vote yes. A pre-vote explanation is consistent with stressing Council unity, condemning Houthi attacks, and clarifying that Houthi actions are not justified by Gaza.

before.Algeria: Mr. President, Algeria will vote in favour of this draft. We welcome the inclusion of the call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza and the clear reaffirmation of the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of Yemen and other States in the region. We also note the balanced language stating that nothing in this resolution authorizes the use of force against the territory of any State and that any measures taken must fully respect sovereignty and international law. Algeria reiterates its demand that the Houthis cease attacks on shipping, release the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel, and that all parties act with maximum restraint. We stress that any exercise of the right to self-defence must be proportionate, must not undermine the sovereignty of States, and must not replace diplomacy or the United Nations-led Yemeni-owned peace process. The Council must remain focused on addressing root causes, including the situation in Gaza, and on protecting civilians and humanitarian access throughout Yemen.
before.China: Mr. President, China has consistently held that the Red Sea is an important international trade and energy corridor. We condemn the attacks on commercial vessels and call on the Houthis to cease such attacks, respect international law, and release the Galaxy Leader and its crew as well as all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel. At the same time, the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of Yemen and other coastal States must be respected. The Security Council should not authorize the use of force, and all measures must conform to international law and the Charter and avoid further escalation. We welcome that the draft reflects these concerns, along with the call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza and a United Nations-led Yemeni political process. China will vote in favour of the draft resolution and hopes it will be implemented in a balanced and effective manner.
before.Denmark: Denmark votes in favour of this draft resolution. We thank the penholders for their efforts to produce a balanced text that responds to the grave threats to maritime security in the Red Sea while upholding international law, the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and the coastal States, and the central role of the United Nations-led political process. Denmark strongly condemns the continued Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels and against civilian infrastructure, and we call for the immediate and unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and of all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained. At the same time, we emphasize that all military actions must conform to international law, including the Charter of the United Nations and international humanitarian law, and must avoid further escalation. Denmark remains deeply concerned by the humanitarian situation in Yemen and the broader region, and we underline the need for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, accountability, and a comprehensive, inclusive and Yemeni-led political settlement with the full and meaningful participation of women. We also reiterate the importance of full implementation of the targeted arms embargo and of intensified diplomatic efforts, including an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, to address the root causes of regional instability.
before.France: France votes in favour of this resolution. We welcome a balanced and operational text that condemns in the strongest terms the Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels and civilian infrastructure, calls for the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel, and reaffirms the targeted arms embargo. France stresses that all measures taken must be in full conformity with international law, including the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and other coastal States, and must avoid further regional escalation. Freedom of navigation and maritime security must be protected. We also underline the need for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access in Yemen and for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza. France remains firmly committed to the United Nations-led political process and to a comprehensive, inclusive, Yemeni-led settlement.
before.Greece: Greece will vote in favour of this draft resolution. As a maritime nation with a fundamental interest in the safety of seafarers, freedom of navigation and the stability of global trade routes, Greece strongly condemns the continued Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels, civilian infrastructure and the territory of States in the region. We call for the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and of all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained. At the same time, this text is carefully balanced: it demands restraint, reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and coastal States, stresses that nothing in the resolution authorizes the use of force, and reaffirms the inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter. Greece supports the emphasis on full implementation of the targeted arms embargo, unhindered humanitarian access, protection of civilians, and a comprehensive Yemeni-led political settlement under United Nations auspices. We also stress the need for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza as an essential element of regional de-escalation. Greece therefore supports this resolution as a measured and lawful response to a serious threat to international peace and security.
before.Guyana: Guyana will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We support its clear condemnation of continued Houthi attacks against commercial and merchant vessels and civilian infrastructure, its demand for the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel, and its reaffirmation of the targeted arms embargo. At the same time, we welcome the text's emphasis that all measures must fully conform to international law and the Charter of the United Nations, respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and other coastal States, and avoid further escalation. We reiterate the need to address root causes, including an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, and to support the United Nations-led Yemeni peace process.
before.Pakistan: Pakistan will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We condemn attacks on merchant and commercial vessels, which threaten freedom of navigation, maritime security and global supply chains. At the same time, the Council must uphold the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of Yemen and all coastal States, and must oppose any military action that violates international law or further escalates regional tensions. We support the draft’s affirmation that all measures must conform to the Charter, including the principle of non-intervention and respect for the inherent right of self-defence. The humanitarian situation in Yemen requires urgent, safe and unhindered access, and detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel must be released immediately. Pakistan also stresses that the situation in Gaza is a root cause of regional instability; an immediate and permanent ceasefire there is essential. We support the United Nations-led Yemeni peace process and call on all parties to engage in good faith towards an inclusive political settlement.
before.Panama: Panama votes in favour of this resolution. As a maritime State that depends on and believes in the rule of law at sea, Panama strongly condemns the continued attacks on merchant and commercial vessels and on civilian infrastructure, and we call for the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader, its crew, and all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel. We also stress the importance of freedom of navigation, the safety of seafarers, full respect for international law including the Charter, and restraint by all parties. Panama would have preferred an explicit reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the rights of flag States, but we support this text as a necessary contribution to de-escalation, humanitarian access, and a political solution in Yemen and the region.
before.Republic of Korea: Thank you, Mr. President. The Republic of Korea will vote in favour of this draft resolution. We strongly condemn the continued Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels and civilian infrastructure, which threaten freedom of navigation, the safety of seafarers and global supply chains. We support the demands for the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and of all United Nations and humanitarian personnel detained by the Houthis, as well as the full implementation of the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015). We also welcome the text’s reaffirmation of international law, sovereignty and territorial integrity, the inherent right of self-defence, restraint, humanitarian access and the need for a comprehensive Yemeni-led political process under United Nations auspices. We urge all parties to avoid further escalation and to pursue dialogue.
before.Russian Federation:
Mr. President,

The Russian Federation will abstain in the voting on the draft resolution submitted by Greece and co-sponsored by the United States.

We note that some of our proposals have been taken into account. The dangerous reference to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea has been removed, a call for a ceasefire in Gaza has been included, and the text now contains a general condemnation of unlawful military strikes against the territory of States, including Yemen. We welcome these changes.

However, serious concerns remain. The draft still affirms a right to defend vessels and reaffirms Article 51 self-defence in a manner that could be exploited to justify further illegal military action against Yemen. The text also fails to clearly name those responsible for the unlawful strikes against Yemeni territory, including by the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. We cannot accept any ambiguity that might be used to legitimize aggression under the pretext of protecting navigation.

The Russian Federation supports the demand that the Houthis cease attacks on commercial vessels and release the Galaxy Leader and its crew. We also support the need for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and a political settlement in Yemen. But the current text remains unbalanced. That is why we will abstain.
before.Sierra Leone: Sierra Leone thanks the penholders for their continued efforts and constructive engagement. We remain gravely concerned by the continued Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels, which threaten freedom of navigation, the safety of seafarers and regional and global supply chains. At the same time, we welcome the balanced text before the Council, which addresses the need to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and other coastal States, urges restraint and compliance with international law, calls for humanitarian access, reinforces the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015), and recognizes the importance of addressing root causes, including the situation in Gaza and the Yemeni peace process. For these reasons, Sierra Leone will vote in favour of the draft resolution.
before.Somalia: Somalia votes in favour of this draft resolution. We do so because it responds to the grave threat posed by continued attacks on merchant and commercial vessels in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, which endanger freedom of navigation, seafarers, and global supply chains. We strongly support the demands for the immediate cessation of such attacks and the unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader, its crew, and all arbitrarily detained United Nations and humanitarian personnel. Somalia also welcomes the resolution’s reaffirmation of the sovereignty, territorial integrity, political independence, and unity of Yemen and of the coastal States of the Red Sea, and its clear affirmation that nothing in this text authorizes the use of force against any State. We emphasize the need for all measures to be consistent with international law, including the Charter of the United Nations, and to avoid further escalation. We further support the call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, the need for full humanitarian access in Yemen, and a comprehensive, inclusive, Yemeni-led and Yemeni-owned political process under United Nations auspices. We also welcome the emphasis on capacity-building for coastal States in maritime domain awareness and maritime security, which is essential for regional stability.
before.United Kingdom of Great Britain and Nort: Thank you, Mr President. The United Kingdom welcomes the revisions made to this draft, including the clear affirmation that Houthi attacks against shipping are illegal and unjustified and cannot be justified by the situation in Gaza, as well as the reaffirmation of the inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter. Houthi attacks continue to threaten freedom of navigation, the safety of seafarers, and global food and energy security. We call for their immediate cessation, the immediate and unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew, and the release of all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained by the Houthis. We support full implementation of the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216, respect for the inviolability of United Nations premises, and renewed efforts toward a comprehensive political settlement in Yemen. The United Kingdom interprets this resolution as preserving the inherent right of self-defence and as not authorizing the use of force, and we will vote in favour.
before.United States of America: The United States thanks Greece for its leadership and is proud to co-sponsor this resolution. We will vote in favour. The Council must speak clearly and with one voice in condemning the Houthis’ continued and unlawful attacks on merchant and commercial vessels, on civilian infrastructure, and on the territory of regional States. This text also demands the immediate release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and all United Nations and humanitarian personnel arbitrarily detained by the Houthis, and it reinforces the obligation of all Member States to implement the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015). Let me be clear: Houthi attacks against shipping are illegal and unjustified and cannot be justified by the situation in Gaza. At the same time, the United States welcomes the text’s reaffirmation that nothing in this resolution authorizes the use of force against the territory of any State and that the inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter is fully preserved, including the right of States to defend their vessels and personnel from attack consistent with international law. We urge all Council members to support this resolution.

after.Greece:
Mr. President,

Greece thanks all Council members for their constructive engagement and welcomes the adoption of this resolution by 14 votes in favour. As a maritime nation, Greece believes the Council has today sent a clear and necessary message: the Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels, against civilian infrastructure and against the territory of States in the region are illegal, unacceptable and must stop immediately. The safety of seafarers, freedom of navigation and the stability of global supply chains are core interests of my country, and they are also interests of this Council as a whole.

Greece notes that the text is carefully balanced. It demands the immediate and unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew and of all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained by the Houthis. It reaffirms the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 and calls for its full implementation. It upholds the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of Yemen and the coastal States. It stresses that nothing in this resolution authorizes the use of force, while reaffirming the inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter. It calls for restraint, proportionality, compliance with international law and unhindered humanitarian access. And it recognizes the need to address root causes, including an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza and support for the United Nations-led Yemeni peace process.

We regret that the Council could not speak with complete unanimity today, but the breadth of support for this text is significant. Greece will continue to engage with all members to ensure that this resolution is implemented in full and in good faith, and that this Council remains actively seized of the matter. Thank you.
after.Slovenia:
Mr. President,

Slovenia voted in favour of this resolution and welcomes its adoption. We thank Greece and the United States for their efforts to produce a balanced text that responds to the grave threat to maritime security in the Red Sea while upholding international law.

As a maritime country, Slovenia attaches particular importance to freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers. We unequivocally condemn the Houthi attacks against merchant and commercial vessels and against civilian infrastructure. They must cease. We demand the immediate and unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader, its crew, and all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained by the Houthis.

At the same time, Slovenia stresses that all measures taken by Member States must be in full conformity with international law and the Charter, including international humanitarian and human rights law. They must respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Yemen and other coastal States and avoid further escalation. We read this resolution as not authorizing the use of force against any State; any exercise of the inherent right of self-defence must be within the strict limits of Article 51 and international law. We also emphasize the need for full, safe and unhindered humanitarian access and for accountability for violations.

Finally, we reaffirm the need for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza and for addressing root causes, including through the United Nations-led Yemeni peace process. The Council must remain actively seized of this matter, and we will continue to support diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and protect civilians.
after.United States of America:
Mr. President,

The United States welcomes the adoption of this resolution and thanks Greece for its leadership in steering the Council to a strong and balanced text. We also thank the members that voted in favour. The message of this Council is clear: the Houthis’ attacks against merchant and commercial vessels, civilian infrastructure, and the territory of regional States are unlawful, unacceptable, and must stop.

The United States will continue to work with partners to protect freedom of navigation and the safety of seafarers in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, consistent with international law, including the inherent right of self-defence under Article 51 of the Charter. We reiterate our demand for the immediate and unconditional release of the M/V Galaxy Leader and its crew, as well as all United Nations personnel and humanitarian workers arbitrarily detained by the Houthis.

This resolution also rightly reinforces the obligation of all Member States to implement the targeted arms embargo under resolution 2216 (2015). We urge all Member States to take that obligation seriously. At the same time, the United States supports the calls in this text for restraint, de-escalation, humanitarian access, and a comprehensive political solution in Yemen under United Nations auspices. Houthi attacks against shipping cannot be justified by the situation in Gaza, and they must not be allowed to derail diplomacy or deepen regional instability. The United States remains committed to working with this Council to advance maritime security and a durable peace in Yemen.
